name: Tesla Powerwall 3 Home Battery
summary: The benchmark installed home battery, especially if you are adding solar at the same time.
verdict: The Powerwall 3 is what most people picture when they think of a house battery, and its specifications explain why. Tesla rates it at 13.5kWh of usable storage and 11.5kW of continuous output, which is enough in a single unit to run most of a typical home, including many central air conditioners, during an outage. Unlike earlier Powerwalls, it has a solar inverter built in, so a new solar-plus-storage system needs one less piece of equipment, and Tesla's DC expansion units add more storage without adding another inverter. It uses LFP chemistry. You cannot buy it online and install it yourself; it is sold and installed through Tesla and certified installers, who also supply the backup gateway or switch that isolates the house from the grid. That makes the price a quote, not a list number, and it is usually best value when solar is part of the same project.
pros: 11.5kW continuous output is the highest single-unit rating here
Built-in solar inverter saves a box on new solar installs
DC expansion units add storage without another inverter
Mature app and widely available installer network
Whole-home backup possible with Tesla's backup hardware
cons: Price set by local installer, often well into five figures
Best value when bought alongside new solar

name: Enphase IQ Battery 5P Home Battery
summary: The right battery if your roof already runs on Enphase microinverters.
verdict: Enphase builds its battery the way it builds its solar: in small, modular pieces. Each IQ Battery 5P stores 5kWh and is rated by Enphase for 3.84kW of continuous output and 7.68kW of short-term peak, and units stack, so two give you 10kWh and roughly double the output, three give you 15kWh and so on. That makes it easy to size precisely, starting small and adding more later. It is AC-coupled and uses LFP cells, and it pairs most cleanly with homes already running Enphase microinverters, where the whole system lives in one app. Backup requires Enphase's IQ System Controller, which handles the grid isolation. Like the Powerwall, it is sold only through installers. The trade-off for the modularity is that matching a single Powerwall 3 takes several units, and the per-kWh cost can climb as you stack them.
pros: Modular 5kWh steps let you buy exactly what you need
Natural fit for homes with Enphase microinverters
LFP chemistry with a long warranty
3.84kW continuous and 7.68kW peak per unit, per Enphase
Multiple units add both storage and output
cons: Needs several units to match one Powerwall
Whole-home backup requires the IQ System Controller

name: FranklinWH aPower 2 Home Battery
summary: The installed battery to choose when you also want a generator in the plan.
verdict: FranklinWH is the least famous of the three installed brands and arguably the most flexible. The aPower 2 is rated at 15kWh of storage and 10kW of continuous output per unit, putting it in the same class as the Powerwall 3 with a little more capacity per box. The real draw is the aGate, the controller that sits between the battery, the grid, the house and any solar. It is designed to work with solar from other manufacturers and includes a dedicated input for a standby or portable generator, so a battery-plus-generator system can be managed from one box rather than with improvised switching. That makes it a strong choice for rural homes that see long outages and want the generator to step in automatically when the battery runs low. It is sold through certified installers only, so availability and price depend on who serves your area.

10kW continuous output handles heavy loads

name: Bluetti AC500 Power Station with B300S Battery
summary: A sensible modular system for homes that do not need 240V.
verdict: The Bluetti AC500 is a modular system: a 5,000W inverter head that pairs with separate B300S battery packs, each rated at 3,072Wh of LFP storage. Bluetti states up to six B300S packs per AC500, for about 18.4kWh, so you can start with one or two and add more as needed. Because the inverter and batteries are separate boxes, each piece is lighter and easier to move than a single giant unit, which matters if you have stairs between the garage and the basement. The limitation is voltage: the AC500 is a 120V system, so it cannot run a well pump, electric dryer or central air on its own. Bluetti sells a separate box to combine two units for 240V output, but at that point one of the native 240V systems above is usually the simpler buy. For a gas-heated house on city water, it is a capable, flexible backup.

B300S batteries add storage in about 3kWh steps
Up to 18.4kWh with six B300S, per Bluetti

Often cheaper per kWh than 240V systems
cons: Older platform than the other plug-in picks
